data.title: Pointer
data.tagline: A value holding a target location so a program can find data through that location
data.learningOutcome: Distinguish shared contents from independent copies, and ask AI to verify that editing and cancelling preserves the original configuration.
data.description: When two names point to the same settings object, editing its contents changes what both names read. JavaScript object references help illustrate this relationship, but do not expose directly manipulable memory addresses.

learning.assumes: Have used settings forms with Save and Cancel; no knowledge of memory addresses is needed.
learning.outcome: Distinguish shared contents from independent copies, and ask AI to verify that editing and cancelling preserves the original configuration.

distinctions.label: Object reference
distinctions.explanation: JavaScript object references let multiple names access one object and can be illustrated with pointer arrows. They are not raw pointers for directly reading or writing memory addresses, or equivalent to pointers in every language.

distinctions.label: Mouse and touch pointer
distinctions.explanation: A visible Cursor and input pointers in Pointer Events locate mouse, touch, or pen input. They are not the data Pointer explained here; CSS pointer-events does not operate on memory.

explanation.title: Editing contents versus changing targets
explanation.text: Updating draft.theme.mode changes the object it reaches. Assigning a different object to draft only changes that name’s target; it does not rewrite the original object. Assigning primitive values such as numbers also differs from sharing mutable objects.

explanation.title: Shallow copying isolates only the first level
explanation.text: { ...original } creates a new outer object, but theme still points to the original theme object. Updating draft.theme.mode therefore still affects the original. Unlike direct assignment, the outer objects are now separate.

explanation.title: What pointers mean in Git
explanation.text: A Git branch records its target commit. Usually HEAD points to the current branch, which points to a commit. This is a target-recording analogy, not a memory address. Switching branches also updates working-tree files and may be blocked by uncommitted edits. Not duplicating the whole project does not mean files remain unchanged.

data.boundary: Deep copying is not the only solution: copying the edited parts or storing draft fields separately can also work. structuredClone supports specific types; an object containing a function throws an error. Ask AI to inspect the data first. Copying an already-mutated object cannot recover its original contents.

lessonPractice.title: The settings contain a nested theme object. After creating a draft with { ...original }, you set draft.theme.mode to dark. What happens to original.theme.mode?

options.label: It also becomes dark because both outer objects share theme
options.feedback: A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but does not copy the nested theme. Updating its mode affects what both names read.

options.label: It stays light because the draft has a new outer object
options.feedback: A separate outer object isolates top-level replacement. This edit changes the still-shared theme object.

options.label: It changes from light to dark only when Cancel is clicked
options.feedback: The shared object changes when its property is edited. Cancel is not the trigger.

data.agentPrompt: Editing settings and cancelling also changes the original configuration. Check whether the draft shares the original or nested objects, then isolate edits in a way appropriate to the data types. Verify that editing nested fields and cancelling preserves the original, and that settings update only on Save.
